meeting_header: Date: 2025-04-02 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: 47 minutes | Attendees: Liam Rodriguez (Redwood AE), Priya Nandakumar (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Ember), Mark D'Angelo (Ember Eng), Rachel Kim (Ember Security), Tom Brooks (Ember CTO)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Ember Ventures through cost sensitivity techniques (prefetch, KV/prefix caching, batching) and the Redwood Console Optimize recommendations. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and per-token cost; compared hosted vs dedicated for Ember's bursty traffic; agreed to run a short benchmark and share a tailored cost model spreadsheet. Security team requested SOC2/KMS docs and SSO checklist.
topics: Prefetch strategy and pre-warming vs on-demand generation
Prefix/KV cache mechanics and warm cache hit rates
Batching windows, concurrency, and tail latency tradeoffs
Console walkthrough: per-route cost breakdowns and optimize recommendations
Hosted vs Dedicated cost profile for Ember's traffic shape
Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, VPC peering, SSO/SAML
transcript:
[00:00:01] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Liam from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our SE.
[00:00:12] Priya: hi all, quick: i'll run through the optimize playbook and then show the console so you can see where recommendations land.
[00:00:24] Sofia: awesome, we care mostly about cost per 1k responses and keeping latency under 400ms 95th for our chat endpoints.
[00:00:38] Mark: and we get bursts during campaign spikes so predictable tail behavior matters.
[00:00:52] Priya: totally — we'll cover batching, prefix/kv cache and prefetching; quick note, our KV cache is prefix-aware so it handles session-like tokens well but warm up matters.
[00:01:10] Liam: for context, Ember's sample: average prompt 120 tokens, average generation 90 tokens, and more system prefixes for personalization.
[00:01:28] Rachel: security question up front: do you support customer-managed KMS and HSM for keys and can we keep logs in our VPC?
[00:01:40] Priya: yes we support KMS integrations; private deployments or VPC peering for logs — I'll drop the SOC2 + KMS doc after.
[00:01:52] Tom: what's the delta between hosted and dedicated on unit cost if we do heavy caching?
[00:02:05] Liam: great question — rough rule: hosted gives fastest onboarding but higher list price; dedicated amortizes GPU and networking so per-token drops as you increase concurrency and cache hit-rates. i'll show a worked example.
[00:02:22] Priya: jumping into the console now — (screen share noises) — here's Optimize > Recommendations. you can see suggested batch window and prefix TTL based on your historical seq lengths. note these are default starting points.
[00:02:45] Mark: i see a 'prefetch weight' slider — what's that?
[00:02:52] Priya: the prefetch weight controls how aggressively we speculatively warm KV cache for likely next tokens / continuations. higher weight reduces cold-start tok generation but increases compute for prefetches.
[00:03:10] Liam: example: if you prefetch 1 token ahead for 20% of requests you may reduce end-user latency by ~30–40ms but you pay a small extra per-request compute.
[00:03:28] Sofia: can you quantify 'small' — we need to map to $/1k calls.
[00:03:35] Priya: sure — on our sample model, prefetching one token on 20% of calls increased token ops by ~6% but reduced tail latency; in the sheet we'll translate that to $ per 1k and show break even vs SLA penalties.
[00:03:55] Liam: here's a quick spreadsheet view (links in chat: deck, cost-model csv).
[00:04:10] Mark: the console shows cache hit % over time — is that prefix hit or full KV hits?
[00:04:19] Priya: prefix hits — we surface both prefix and KV cache hits; prefix is an L1, KV is the larger L2. prefix hits are super cheap.
[00:04:32] Tom: is the prefix deterministic? what if the user has dynamic system prompts?
[00:04:40] Priya: prefix matching is fuzzy to allow small variations; you can configure exact matches for high-value sessions and use tokenized prefix fingerprints for more flexible matching.
[00:04:56] Rachel: on compliance, you mentioned audit logs — can we push logs to our SIEM?
[00:05:05] Liam: yes, audit and request-level logs can be forwarded via secure syslog/S3 sinks; in Private deployments logs remain in your network.
[00:05:16] Sofia: the playbook mentioned batching window adjustments — how do we tune without hurting latency?
[00:05:25] Priya: there are two knobs: batch max-wait (ms) and batch size cap. for low-latency apps we recommend shallow batch windows (e.g., 8–12ms) plus concurrency increase; for high-throughput backends you can increase batch windows to 25–50ms to gain compute efficiency.
[00:05:45] Mark: how does concurrency interact with prefetch? if we prefetch aggressively will batches fill with speculative tokens?
[00:05:54] Priya: speculative prefetches are accounted separately; they don't block real request tokens but they do consume GPU cycles. the scheduler prioritizes live requests over speculative work.
[00:06:10] Liam: here's a concrete scenario: Ember does 200 RPS with 5% spikes to 800 RPS for 60s. with prefix cache hit-rate at 40% and a modest batch window (12ms) savings are X; i'll put numbers in the sheet.
[00:06:29] (00:06:30] Sofia: slight crosstalk — sorry go ahead.
[00:06:38] Priya: no worries — also note continuous batching benefits more when sequence lengths are similar; high variance reduces batching efficiency.
[00:06:50] Mark: can we pin model versions across hosted and dedicated?
[00:06:57] Liam: yes — same API surface. you can pin to a version and our routing will fall back to compatible variants if capacity is constrained.
[00:07:10] Priya: (shows console cost breakdown) on the per-route chart you can break down token costs by prompt vs completion vs prefetch ops.
[00:07:24] Rachel: i see 'privacy mode' in settings — what does it scrub?
[00:07:31] Priya: privacy mode omits request text from logs and stores only token counts and embeddings if enabled — good for sensitive workloads.
[00:07:44] Tom: for the benchmark you mentioned, do you need us to provide sample prompts and a session churn profile?
[00:07:52] Liam: yes please — the more representative the dataset, the better. Priya can run hosted+dedicated and we'll return the raw traces.
[00:08:04] Priya: switching to the cost model: there are three levers — batching, cache hit-rate, and quantization/instance type. quantization reduces per-token GPU ops but may slightly affect output quality.
[00:08:20] Mark: have you seen quality regressions from quantization with our class of LLMs?
[00:08:26] Priya: for most instruction-following small-medium models, 4-bit quantization with the right kernels is near parity; we'll annotate any known regressions in the model catalog.
[00:08:38] Sofia: how do we tune prefix TTL? longer TTL = more hits but risk stale personalization, right?
[00:08:46] Priya: exactly — TTL is workload dependent. our console suggests initial TTL per route and you can create rules: e.g., personal session prefixes TTL 30m, ephemeral prompts TTL 5m.
[00:08:59] Liam: i'll highlight an optimization: group users by prompt fingerprinting to increase cross-user prefix reuse for system prompts that are common. that reduces cold starts without affecting personalized parts.
[00:09:13] Rachel: if we do Private deployment, do you support customer-managed HSM and audit key rotation?
[00:09:20] Priya: yes — private deploy supports HSM and audit key rotation; we'll connect your security team with infra eng to map requirements.
[00:09:32] Mark: show us the end-to-end of an A/B rollout to test a more aggressive prefetch policy.
[00:09:38] Priya: (navigates) rollouts -> canary -> choose route -> set prefetch delta. you can do a canary to 10% traffic for 24h and the console will compute cost delta and failure metrics.
[00:09:55] Tom: do you have guardrails to auto-roll back if latency spikes?
[00:10:00] Priya: yes, you can set SLO thresholds (latency, error) and an automatic rollback policy.
[00:10:07] Liam: ok moving to a worked example — i've got three columns: baseline (no prefetch, TTL 0), conservative prefetch (20% at 1 token, TTL 5m), aggressive prefetch (50% at 2 tokens, TTL 20m).
[00:10:23] Sofia: and the cost difference?
[00:10:26] Liam: baseline $8 per 1k; conservative $8.48 per 1k (+6%); aggressive $9.6 per 1k (+20%) but reduces 95th latency by ~120ms in our sim.
[00:10:40] Mark: that 120ms seems large — is that for cold cache workloads?
[00:10:45] Priya: it's for mixed workloads with 30% cold sessions; for warm cache only the delta is ~20–30ms.
[00:10:55] Rachel: how do you attribute cost back to product teams? can the console break down by API key / token?
[00:11:02] Priya: yes — per-token accounting by API key, route, model, and you can tag requests for chargeback.
[00:11:12] Tom: about capacity — if we go dedicated, whats the minimum commit?
[00:11:18] Liam: typical Dedicated starts with a monthly reserve for X GPUs; i'll include the exact bands in the pricing spreadsheet. we have burst options too to cover spikes.
[00:11:30] (00:11:32] Sofia: slight filler — sorry.
[00:11:40] Mark: does prefix caching work across model versions when you pin?
[00:11:47] Priya: prefix cache entries are model-version aware; you can enable cross-version compatibility for small model deltas but we don't assume semantic parity by default.
[00:11:59] Rachel: will you provide a data retention table? we need specifics for GDPR and logs.
[00:12:05] Liam: yes — retention options and deletion flows included in the security doc; we'll send the table.
[00:12:16] Priya: (screen) final Optimize tip: use conservative prefetch for user-facing sessions and more aggressive for background generative tasks where latency is less critical.
[00:12:32] Sofia: curious on real numbers from other customers — do you have case studies with similar burst shapes?
[00:12:40] Liam: we have an ecommerce customer with similar bursts; I'll anonymize and share the case notes and a before/after cost curve.
[00:12:50] Mark: can the console simulate cost outcomes if we change TTL or prefetch intensity?
[00:12:57] Priya: yes — Modeler -> Scenario simulation: you can input traffic shape, seq length distribution, and we'll estimate token ops and dollars.
[00:13:10] Tom: what's the expected time to run your benchmark?
[00:13:13] Priya: small smoke ~2 hours; representative runs depending on QPS may be 4–6 hours to gather tail stats. we'll schedule the short 2-hour one first.
[00:13:24] (00:13:30] Rachel: question on encryption-in-transit keys for VPC peering?
[00:13:34] Liam: TLS for all traffic; for private peering we use VPN or Direct Connect-style; details in the network appendix i'll send.
[00:13:47] Sofia: any gotchas on embedding generation and caching interplay? we also call embeddings to index content frequently.
[00:13:55] Priya: embeddings are idempotent — we recommend caching embedding vectors at the application layer and invalidating on content changes. the console can show embedding call rates and cost.
[00:14:10] Mark: one last thing — for the A/B canary, can we route only based on headers?
[00:14:17] Priya: yes you can do header-based routing or percent-based; flexible matcher.
[00:14:25] Liam: ok we're at the demo wrap — quick recap: we'll send the cost model, priya runs bench, ember provides sample prompts, and security gets SOC2 + KMS docs.
[00:14:37] Sofia: sounds good — also can you include an expected ROI table for 3, 6, 12 months?
[00:14:44] Liam: yes, i'll include that.
[00:14:50] Mark: thanks, appreciate the clear tradeoffs.
[00:14:55] Rachel: thanks — talk to you soon.
[00:15:00] [END OF RECORDED TRANSCRIPT — rest was Q&A and scheduling small logistics until 15:47]
notes: Links shared in chat: deck (redwood-optimize-playbook.pdf), cost-model.csv, security-docs link: https://redwood.ai/security.pdf
Priya to run hosted vs dedicated smoke benchmark using Ember sample prompts; will upload traces to shared folder
